utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Kenneth Scott for the Office of the Prosecutor. With me are Mr. Douglas Stringer, Mr. Vassily Poriouvaev, Mr. Roeland Bos, and our case manager is Kimberly Fleming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Kresimir Krsnik for Mr. Naletilic, and I have Mr. Christopher Meek from the Bar Association of Kansas, United States, and legal assistant, Nika Pinter, lawyer from Zagreb, the Bar Association of Croatia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm lawyer Branko Seric from Zagreb, a member of the Bar Association of Croatia, and I'm chief counsel for the defendant Vinko Martinovic. With me is co-counsel Vinko Martinovic [as interpreted], lawyer member of the Bar Association of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Naletilic, can you hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone is not switched on for the accused. THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will not ask you the same question every morning, but if there is any problem that you have, please do not hesitate to let us know. How about your health? THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone of the accused is not -- THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] I'm quite all right for the time being. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please take care of yourself, especially at the time of changing of the season at this moment. If you have any problems, please do not hesitate to let us know. THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] My only problem is the length of the session. It will be much easier for me if the proceedings lasted about half as long as envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Mr. Martinovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? THE ACCUSED MARTINOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not ask you the same question each morning, but if there is any problem that you have, please do not hesitate to let us know. You may sit down, please. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. By order of the President of the Tribunal, dated September 7th, 2001, this Trial Chamber is composed of three Judges. Sitting on my right is Honourable Judge Maureen Clark from Ireland. Sitting on my left is Honourable Judge Fatoumata Diarra from Mali. My name is Daqun Liu, the Presiding Judge in this case. I used to be in the Trial Chamber II, sitting with Judge Hunt and Judge Mumba in the Krnojelac case. This Trial Chamber would like to thank Pre-Trial Judge, Judge Wald, for her invaluable contribution to the smooth administration of this case. We would also like to thank Mr. Olivier Fourmy for conducting the depositions and transmitting the record therefore to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before the floor is given to the Prosecution for their opening statement, the Trial Chamber would like to address the parties with regard to some administrative issues of general importance of this trial. We would like to remind both parties that the administration of justice can only be carried out effectively and fairly when both parties to the proceeding undertake to fully cooperate with the Tribunal, and they efficiently carry out instructions given by this Trial Chamber. It is hoped during the forthcoming trial all parties will work together to ensure the efficient and the convivial progression of this case. In December 2000, the Pre-Trial Judge indicated that there would be a ten-week time period set for each side. The Trial Chamber is in full agreement with this time schedule and call upon the parties to adhere to it. With regard to the testimony of witnesses, the Trial Chamber wishes to assure the parties that it will not accept any disrespectable questioning by any of the parties. This applies equally to Prosecution and the Defence witnesses. We have to bear in mind this is an International Tribunal which, at least, means whatever you said will be translated simultaneously into the other two languages. In our view, it is not important of how you perform in this courtroom. What is more important is to let us to understand what you are talking about and to have every word you said correctly recorded in the transcript. So do make a pause after each question and answer during the examination of witnesses or after a paragraph, when you are making a long statement. This Trial Chamber expects the parties to brief their respective witnesses accordingly at the beginning of their testimony. Now, we have some outstanding motions concerning the admission of transcripts and the statements into evidence. At this moment, these issues are under consideration by the Trial Chamber, and decisions will be made with regard to all those related matters. As for the Defence motion under Rule 92(B) dated August 2nd, 2001, concerning the written statements of two witnesses, the Trial Chamber noted that the Prosecution has not responded to it. Are you intending to respond to this motion, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will review it further and make a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will decide on the outstanding motions. Are you ready to proceed with opening statements, in accordance with Rule 84, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Prosecution is ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, wait a minute. Please receive my apologies, Your Honours; however, the Defence deems it necessary to inform the Trial Chamber about some facts which have been -- 15 days ago, likewise, to inform the Chamber about the position of the Defence regarding the main hearing today. In other words, Your Honours, you have informed us very exhaustively with regards to the Defence suggestions which arrived in August; however, we also submitted another motion to postpone the hearing based on the decision of the Chamber following our first motion, and we consider it of key importance. We have also moved for an additional explanation of the ex parte session. We have also moved for an inside visit of the Chamber; that is, to travel to Bosnia-Herzegovina and visit the area that will be discussed here for quite some time. The Defence believes that that motion and the additional motion for the deferral of the hearing are very important, especially since you are the first ones to start the trial without a Pre-Trial Conference which we were duty bound to hold pursuant to the Statute of the Tribunal. Had we had the Pre-Trial Conference, I would not be saying what I am saying today in presenting the positions of the Defence; and at that conference, we would have resolved all the matters in dispute. Why I say all this, Your Honours, because the Defence try not to violate the Article 1 of the Statute of the fair and expeditious trial at which, though, the Defence is concerned that the Article might be violated if we started the proceedings today, because a few days ago, the Defence received - and you can see it here - over 1.000 documents, and it was only a few days ago, which we have to study. We have to be ready; we have to be prepared in order to participate in the examination of witnesses. Likewise, a few days ago, Your Honours, the Defence received the definitive list of witnesses. And it is only for the past few days that we have finally learned which witnesses the Prosecution intended to call. For all these reasons, the Defence does not feel fully prepared to participate in the trial on an equitable footing because it has not had enough time to -- for adequate preparation. And as serious advocates, we cannot permit ourselves to engage in hearing and deliberations before this august World Court without having studied all this material which was disclosed to us only a couple of days before. The Defence wishes to point out that before other Courts, tactics or ruses of any one party may be allowed. Perhaps, something like that is permissible before the lesser Courts, and it is permitted, but not before this Court. And especially, one cannot place the Defence at such a disadvantageous position. Moreover, Your Honours, my learned friends have a huge machinery to support them, and the Defence does not have that. They have at their disposal an unlimited number of investigators. As for the multinational forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the official bodies in both Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and, if you like, the media, too. And we, you see, have to parry, and we are only three -- there is four of us, and we have to do it all by ourselves, Your Honours. One thousand times -- binders are still to be gone through by the Defence. We have gone through a thousand, and we have to go through a another few thousand of similar binders which are in the State archives of Croatia alone. The archive of the Minister of Defence, we may not make it there. The Minister of Foreign Affairs never had time to pass the load. The archives of the duration of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if anything, we still have not received a response from the relevant authorities whether we would have access to this documentation or not. If we are to enjoy an equal status before this Court, we have to go through all this. We must learn every single fact so as to take part in examination or, rather, know what the Prosecution is talking about. That is, today, here, the Prosecutor; tomorrow, the witnesses will be examined -- we haven't slept for the past three days -- to at least leaf through all these documents to see what they are all about. Because otherwise, how do you expect us to parry? And is that fair and well-balanced position? And to conclude, I really do not know, and I am asking this on the record, why all of this insistence to start a trial today? What does a postponement of two months mean for justice? What is more important, justice or time? With all this haste, there was even no time for a Pre-Trial Conference. The Defence holds that nothing must be done at the expense of justice; that time cannot be placed before justice. Your Honours, as you have seen, the submission of the learned friends from the Prosecution was also used in the tactics -- they have also requested for the investigators to be present here and to be heard. We have also submitted a similar motion; that is, that our investigator be present for the duration of the trial here. However, we have not even had time to make our objections to the absence of a Pre-Trial Conference. And with all this investigating team, that makes us question the objectivity. Why should I have called expert witnesses or -- and this Defence considers it indispensable, and asks you to visit the ground, to visit the site where all these events took place. Defence believes that it is absolutely indispensable for the Honourable Judges to see the area. And let me conclude: 60 percent of the indictment refers to the international conflict and alleges that my client is an agent of Croatia in that conflict. If the Prosecutor persists in alleging that, then, Your Honours, we need to submit -- to produce millions of documents, if you wish, for this Defence, and it will always be very straightforward because we are before the World Court of Justice. We who are creating the new law, and we who are participating in the creation of this new law, and all that we say now will be part of the history of international law. So the Defence says, No, we are not ready. And today, we are not ready to stand up to the Prosecutor. And we are requesting at this moment of at least two months so as to prepare for the examination of witnesses, as was customary in this Tribunal before. When the Prosecution closes its case, we should also be given some time before we start off. If our learned friends from the Prosecution see the point and stop insisting that this was an international conflict and that my client was a foreign country's agent, then we would not need all this. We would not need all of this study, because the study of all these millions of documents refers to that part of the indictment and not the other one. And that is all. Thank you very much, Your Honours, for your patience. I hope I will meet with your understanding and sympathy, and I hope you will grant us our motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsnik, for reminding us of those pending motions. Mr. Seric, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, and thank you. The Defence of Vinko Martinovic wishes to point out that there is a problem which appeared when the Prosecution belatedly, in view of the beginning of the trial today, gave us a list of 11 witnesses, and then five days ago, another list of 55 witnesses, so that there was no time for us to prepare for the cross-examination. For this reason, a compromise proposal might be appropriate, because I would not wish to obstruct the beginning of trial today. The Defence of Vinko Martinovic would request an interruption of proceedings after these witnesses are heard, these ten Prosecution witnesses, many of whom may already be here. And this interruption, in our opinion, should be 60 days. That this is not too long is confirmed by the fact that, on the 5th of September, we received 11 binders with thousands of pages which we have not had time to leaf through, never mind analyse and synthesise. These are very important documents for our Defence, especially in view of Rule 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. We confirm that we did receive in time the list for the first ten witnesses; that is some 20 days ago. And in our opinion, there is no reason for these ten witnesses not to be heard now, since I assume they are already here. However, the Prosecutor disclosed a couple of days another list of another 55 witnesses which they intend to call; and in doing so, they have prevented us from preparing for the cross-examination, because if we continue immediately the proceedings, then in view of the way in which we work and the length of the daily hearings, we will simply not be able to prepare for the cross-examination. The same applies to the documents, because the Defence doesn't have time during the trial days themselves to study and read these documents which we consider to be extremely important. In the hope that you will accept this position of the Defence of Vinko Martinovic and make an appropriate ruling, I wish to thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Scott, do you want to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. May it please the Court, Your Honour, it's the Prosecution's position on these issues that the Prosecutor has throughout these Pre-Trial proceedings complied with every rule of the Tribunal, every ruling of the Chamber. Witness statements were provided in this case months, if not years, ago. The documents will show -- the records will show that. In addition to that, some 30 days ago, the notice of the first ten Prosecution witnesses did go out. The Defence have had a full 30 days effectively to prepare to meet those witnesses. We, given some further encouragement from the Chamber, provided an additional full tentative order of our entire Prosecution case witnesses, and we have provided that. We expect that it will take approximately two weeks, perhaps even a bit longer, to go through the first ten witnesses. By the time we will have reached the 11th witness, the Defence teams will have had some three or four weeks of all the Prosecution witness list in the order in which we anticipate calling these witnesses. We submit, Your Honours, this is no different than virtually every other ICTY case. There are extensive lists that go out, and all counsel on all sides have to then prepare their cases as best we can. We don't start trials and then take breaks and prepare for the next batch of witnesses, and stop and prepare for the next batch of witnesses, and stop and prepare for the next batch of witnesses. The Prosecution has made all the disclosures that it has been required to make. And as we pointed out in a recent submission, in fact, we have made many submissions and many disclosures far beyond what the Rules required us to make. And in terms of the documents, there is also an extensive record on the matter of document disclosure. Judge Wald, throughout the Pre-Trial proceedings, I would use the term virtually begged - begged, Your Honours - the Defence counsel to request document discovery under 66(B). They continually refused deliberately, and presumably tactically, to make such a question. That was raised, for instance -- and this is all documented; there's a full record on this in our response to the Defence motion to continue, and I can point the Court briefly to three instances. It was addressed by Judge Wald almost a year and a half ago at a Status Conference on the 16th of May, 2000, in which he suggested that both Defence counsel invoke Rule 66(B). They said they would not. It was raised again with the Pre-Trial Conference with Judge Wald on the 20th of July, 2001, approximately two months ago. Once again, both Defence counsel deliberately and clearly said, "We do not seek such document disclosure." It was raised in the first days of the depositions with Mr. Fourmy on the 24th of July, 2001, and again the Defence made it clear that they were not seeking document disclosure. Let me suggest to the Chamber, respectfully, that this, what the counsel are now saying, or at least what Mr. Krsnik is saying, amounts a bit to, "Please save me from myself." We have now disclosed the exhibits that we intend to use during trial, and if the counsel had, over a year and a half ago, invoked Rule 66(B) and asked for disclosure, they would have gotten it. But to come in now at the first day of trial and now say, "Well, we haven't had these documents to look at," as I submit, Your Honour, is Mr. Krsnik saying, "Save me from myself." The Prosecution is ready to proceed, we have witnesses in The Hague, and we oppose a delay. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I respond, Your Honour, to the positions presented by my learned friend Mr. Scott, because to say the least, they are not fair. We are addressing an International Tribunal, and I think this is something that my learned friend keeps forgetting. He keeps referring to the American trial system. It is not true that the Prosecution has played fully by the rules. It is not our duty to disclose reciprocally, and it is your obligation to disclose in time. Half of these documents have not been translated, Your Honour. How am I going to explain to my client what all this is about and how can he help me? By a series of these small tactical moves, the Defence is placed in an unfair position, and then I am said to be asking to be saved. We are not asking anyone to save us. We are here because of these two men and not because of me. And I'm just saying that, because of all these facts, the Defence is not ready, and that is correct and that is a fact, and I have been very sincere in saying this. And I really don't understand why the Prosecution is insisting so much that we begin today. You have asked us to cooperate, and we have done our best to cooperate always and whenever we could. But we will not cooperate in such a way that that plays against us. Your Honour, I really don't understand why we are having this discussion. If the Defence is saying that we need two months to prepare properly, is that such an unreasonable or irrational request? But we have the facts to support this request here before us. Since my learned friend has referred to Status Conferences, Your Honours, you know that at the last Status Conference I had warned about all that would happen today, and I indicated this to Judge Wald. She thanked me at the time, because this was a month and a half ago, and she told me that I should convey this to the Trial Chamber as soon as it is formed. As soon as the President of this Trial Chamber was elected, I immediately filed this motion with the necessary explanations. I amended that motion, and I still have no response to it. And that is another reason why we cannot begin. I responded immediately. Does that give any justification for the Prosecutor to respond in this way? And all these documents, these files, these pictures, you will see the wide range of possibilities that the Prosecution has. They have taken shots of every inch of land, they can collect documents from whoever they want. But we will be able to come back to that at a later stage. My learned friend, Mr. Scott, it is not me that is at stake here, it is justice that is at stake, and in order to serve justice, we must all be ready. And as an attorney, I've never allowed my client to suffer because of my mistake or because I was not ready. So it is not me that is at stake but global justice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Judge Clark will ask the Prosecution some questions. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scott, I was wondering about the documents that have been just lately served on the Defence. What exactly are those documents? Are they intended to be a bound version of documents that you will be relying on later on, or are they very material to the early witnesses for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They are very material to the early --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour. Your Honour, they are very material to the beginnings of the case. In fact, the very first witness will go through a substantial number of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could they have been furnished to the Defence earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Some of them could have and some of them have been. A good number were disclosed, despite the absence of a request for document disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, as you know, Mr. Scott, I'm new to this Tribunal, and therefore I depend on the Prosecution to keep me right on procedure. What would the normal procedure be in a case of this length in relation to the service of such a large number of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can answer your question, I think best at least for me, by reference to two other cases that I'm most familiar with, and that is the Blaskic case and the Kordic case. In the Blaskic case, there was no advance disclosure of documents. Each exhibit was tendered in court as the document was used. There was no advance disclosure to the Defence whatsoever. Documents came in on a daily basis. In the Kordic case, some documents were disclosed at the beginning of trial, others came in on a daily basis. This Tribunal has adopted a particular disclosure regime primarily under Rule 66, which provides the rules that govern disclosure in this case. Rule 66 gives complete control of that to the Defence. If the Defence chooses to request document disclosure, they can do so. Now, what this Tribunal has done, in its wisdom, in the Plenary of the Judges in making rules, is to make the Rule that if the Defence asks for disclosure, document disclosure under Rule 66(B), then they are obligated, under Rule 67(C), to provide reciprocal document disclosure to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So what you're saying is, in the absence of a request by the Defence to have the Prosecution disclose certain documents, there's no obligation on you to serve them until the trial starts?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And in this case, as there was no request to serve them, you decided, nevertheless, as a matter of convenience to the Defence, to serve them with all the documents on which you hope to rely if they are admissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour has stated my position perhaps better than I just did. In our view, respectfully to counsel, we have done more now than we were required to do. We could have followed the Blaskic method. I could have come before Your Honours every day and tendered a new exhibit every day. And counsel, on the record during the depositions, admitted that. They said, "Mr. Scott is" -- when I put that proposition during the conferences, I said exactly that. Your Honour, there's no secrets here. This has not been a hidden issue. It was discussed before Judge Wald and before Mr. Fourmy, and I specifically said, "The posture that this leaves us in is that we can tender exhibits as we go, without any prior disclosure." Mr. Fourmy, with respect, agreed with me that that was the case, and both Defence counsel on the record agreed with me that that was the case. So in providing these documents now, some at least not ten days but they were made available a week ago Friday, we have done more than we were required to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So your position, as I understand it, Mr. Scott, is the Prosecution has served those documents, even though it's at a relatively late stage, on the Defence in ease of their position so that they would know in advance what documents you were going to call and rely on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That is absolutely right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That doesn't make any material difference to the conduct of the case in relation to the first ten witnesses that you propose to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure about -- forgive me, Your Honour. I don't understand the significance of the last part of your comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Had you not served these documents at all, Mr. Scott, you're in a position to proceed with your first ten witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And the service of these documents, as I understand, in the binders which the Defence have referred to, don't, as I understand it, make any material difference to the conduct of the Prosecution case in relation to calling those ten witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm sorry, that's not correct. I thought I said that a moment ago. They are absolutely material to the first witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood me. The content of the banned documents will refer to the witnesses, but had you not served those documents in advance and you served them as you went along, the position wouldn't materially change?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's exactly right, Your Honour. Forgive me for not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you mind if I ask the Defence what they have to say in response to that particular aspect of the case? Have I stated the case correctly? Do you disagree with that position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree with Your Honour, but I think some clarification is required. What disclosure means in reciprocity, that is precisely what I've been referring to. It enables the Prosecutor, who investigates, who charges and who conducts these proceedings, to engage in tactics. And if the Defence were to disclose our documents - and our turn will come in a couple of months - we first have to study their documents to know which documents we have to oppose. I think that is quite clear. Secondly, Your Honour, the Prosecution told us that they would disclose the documents at the last Status Conference, those that support the indictment. All the documents and statements supporting the indictment, they are obligated to disclose to us. And those are these documents. And secondly and most importantly, half of these have not been translated into Croatian. And even if everything Mr. Scott has said may be correct, that he is entitled to this kind of tactics because this is an International Court, and if he has the evidence, he could have told me about it five years ago, why do we need this secrecy and this maneuvering? Why? But as I was saying, they haven't been translated into Croatian, so how am I going to discuss them with my client in the Detention Unit? A further point: These documents are the basis for the Opening Statement, that is, for the indictment. They are a basis for each of the witnesses. They are a basis for the investigator who is being called as a witness to authenticate these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Krsnik. What I wanted to say to you was: Are you materially disadvantaged by having a collection of documents which won't be used until the witnesses are called? By receiving them at this stage, couldn't you proceed with the opening and the first ten witnesses that you're comfortable with and that you were told were going to be called a month ago? Are you materially disadvantaged in relation to the rest of the case by having these documents now? Now, that's the first question I want to ask you. The other question seems to me arises out of this: that you are making the allegation that these documents were served on you as a tactic to force you to disclose your defence by exchanging documents. Is that what you're saying? You're saying that it's a tactic that the Prosecution is using to furnish you with discovery so that you must reciprocate? That's what's been translated to me. Am I incorrect about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm afraid there's a misunderstanding. I said that the Prosecutor, because of this possibility to disclose envisaged by the Rules, can engage in tactics with the Defence and say, "I won't disclose if you don't disclose to me." But maybe again there's a misunderstanding. However, the documents on which the indictment rests and the witnesses on whom the indictment relies is something that he has to disclose within a reasonable time. That is what the Rule says. And I am saying that half of these documents support the indictment and I should have received them long ago. This has nothing to do with disclosure or with reciprocity. So the Prosecutor keeps saying, "Reciprocity, so we were not obligated." My position is that they were duty bound to disclose to us the documents on which the indictment rests within a reasonable time, and that is the substance of the matter. And we have not received them in due time. And thank you very much for your kindness. I appreciate very much the questions you have put to the Prosecutor, to the Prosecution. Truly, this means a lot to me. And what is most important of all at this point and which needs to be said is that: it's been a year and a half now, and in a spirit of cooperation, I think the Prosecution is obliged to cooperate, because it has unlimited authority, unlimited possibilities, in the history of legal systems in the world. And within the scope of those unlimited possibilities, if someone comes here and spends two years in prison, it is very difficult to say that this may not be within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. And this is something that the Defence is opposed to and is saying, "You have no right to this kind of tactics." After all, this is a different kind of court. And the Defence is saying if we had received all this on time -- but let me say finally: Why did we receive ten witnesses 20 days ago and then 55 three days ago? The Prosecution was not aware of this final list of witnesses a month ago? Isn't that tactics?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you there? I think that all of us are aware that getting witnesses together is very difficult from your jurisdiction to here because of historical reasons. What I really want to know at this stage, and I don't want to cut you short in any way - I know that what you're saying is very important - but what I really want to say is: Are you seriously prejudiced if the Prosecution were to open the case, open the facts to the Tribunal, and to call the witnesses that you've had notice of for quite some time, and that maybe the other Judges and I will confer in relation to what happens later? You're not seriously prejudiced in relation to that case, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I would be seriously prejudiced. That is the problem. Surely you don't think that I would be wasting your precious time by saying all this. There was no single reason for us to discuss this today here and now. utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Counsel, ladies and gentlemen. On the 17th of April, 1993, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was on the cutting edge of ethnic cleansing. The president of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban had issued an ultimatum to the Bosnian Muslims, and Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was there to carry it out, to execute the ultimatum. He commanded the Croatian Defence Council Forces attack on the Villages of Sovici and Doljani in central Herzegovina. He presided over the expulsion of Bosnian Muslim civilians from their homes and from their villages. He presided over the burning of their homes and the destruction of their mosques. He presided over the burning of the mosque in both towns, Sovici and Doljani, and he commanded and set the example in the interrogation and beating of Muslim men taken prisoner. The evidence will show that Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and his troops, the Convicts' Battalion, was right in the thick of it, right where they would so often be in the bloody months ahead, when Bosnian Muslims were thrown out of their homes, when their men were killed, when their property was looted and destroyed, and their prisoners treated brutally and inhumanely. After the attack on Sovici and Doljani was completed, many of the Bosnian Muslim prisoners were taken to Tuta's field headquarters at a fish farm in Doljani. There, they were repeatedly beaten and abused, both by Tuta personally, by his senior officers, and by his soldiers. The evidence will show that Tuta threatened prisoners with a pistol, that he put a pistol in one or more prisoner's mouth or to their heads, and he told them, "Lie down and kiss Croatian ground." Only a few weeks later, on the 10th of May, 1993, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, stood victorious in the city of Mostar where he received before him captured Muslim men and arrested Muslim men. Tuta stood before them and swore at the Muslim prisoners. He used the racial insult, which I would not use myself, but to quote the word attributed to the accused Tuta, he insulted their "balija mothers," and he personally beat one of the prisoners with his Motorola radio; again, in front of his officers and men, this is the example he set. There was also another man who would play a role, a key role, in the Croatian Defence Council's continuing attacks and expulsions in Mostar and the surrounding area. One of Mladen Naletilic, Tuta's, commanders, the other accused, Vinko Martinovic, Stela. A Muslim prisoner will tell you that he was twice taken to the front line in Mostar to work for Vinko Martinovic's unit. And on the first occasion, the prisoner was beaten by Martinovic himself, and Martinovic told the prisoner, "I am the one called Stela, and you are going to see who Stela is." In the midst of brutal treatment of Bosnian Muslim prisoners who were taken for forced labour at Stela's frontline area, you will hear how Vinko Martinovic, Stela, said to them, "You have come to work for me." Good morning, Your Honours. Again, my name is Kenneth Scott. I am the senior trial attorney representing the Prosecution in this case. It is both my privilege and my responsibility to present to you the Prosecution case. As I have introduced already, but I will introduce to you briefly again, with me, and as very substantial participants in this trial, will be Mr. Douglas Stringer, Mr. Vassily Poriouvaev, Mr. Roeland Bos. Again, our case manager is Ms. Kimberley Fleming. Presenting these cases, Your Honours can understand, present a number of challenges. One of these is the simple volume of information. A particular aspect of this is the names of the various states, the names of governments, organizations, armies, political parties, treaties, persons, events, and places. It would probably not be very helpful or interesting if I were to stand here for the next few minutes and simply go through a list of names and terms, so I won't do that. The Prosecutor has, however, prepared a glossary which may be helpful to the Chamber and to other participants and staff in the trial. That has previously been provided to the Defence counsel, and I will make that glossary -- if it has not already, make that glossary available to the Chamber now. In addition to that, Your Honours, I will try -- I will do my best to try to stop and define or explain some of the more common terms as we go forward. The case, of course, as the name of this Tribunal indicates, concerns events in the former Yugoslavia. I would, therefore, like to spend a few minutes going over several maps or diagrams which the Prosecution has prepared and will make available to the Chamber and, of course, to counsel for what assistance they may provide. We have brought with us -- excuse me, Your Honour -- two large maps, one which has been marked for identification as Prosecution Exhibit P1, which you can see is a map of the entire former Yugoslavia. And the other second, if you will, hard-mounted map, is a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We fully realize that these maps that I have shown you now are not terribly useful in terms of illustrating something over the distance from the witness stand to where Your Honours are seated, and we are mindful of that. However, we do make these maps available for such use during the course of this trial, as they may be helpful. While we consider them Prosecution exhibits, we certainly make them available for Defence counsel as well, if that will assist them. In addition to these large maps, we have some smaller maps which are probably easier to work with on a day-to-day basis. They also have the virtue that they can be placed on this device called the ELMO, and then everyone can have them on their computer screens. For instance, as an example, with the Court's permission and understanding, I will try to do as much of this myself to save the usher running back and forth and to make the presentation as smooth as possible. This is simply another version of one of the maps in front of Your Honours, which again, in a smaller version which each Judge can put in his or her own file, or what have you, and it has the virtue of being on -- being put on the ELMO and we can go, we can enlarge and go in and out on the map. That is just simply one of the tools. Now, to begin to zero in, Your Honours, on the particular parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina that most relate to this case, we have Exhibit P3.1. The municipalities, and that is a political unit in the former Yugoslavia or Bosnia -- I suppose in other countries, we might call them states or cantons or provinces, or perhaps even counties -- these are the particular units, the municipalities or opstinas, that most directly relate to this Tuta/Stela case. And you will see that, and for point of reference, since more people tend to be familiar, perhaps at least initially, with the city of Sarajevo, you can see what parts of the country we are talking about with the largest city in that area, which we will talk about extensively, being the city of Mostar. I might also say here what the Court will come to understand, if it does not already, is sometimes it is talking about the municipality as a whole, that is the name or word, and sometimes it may refer to a particular town or city. For instance, Mostar is both a city and a municipality. There is the large municipality or state or county that is marked here in red. That is the municipality of Mostar. But within Mostar, you also have the city of Mostar. The same can be said for Siroki Brijeg, which was formerly known as Listica, but renamed Siroki Brijeg. There is both the municipality of Siroki Brijeg, that is the larger political subdivision, and there is also the town of Siroki Brijeg. Important to this case in a number of respects, including the fact that the accused Tuta's headquarters was in Siroki Brijeg. I'll next orient Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were talking about some maps, and I want to, I think, do two more for now. We also have a somewhat larger version - not this size but perhaps A3 size - but also this size of this map, which again may assist the Chamber in terms of locations critical to the case. And in fact, there is an additional separate version. I'm just trying to make the Chamber aware of the tools that will be available. It actually looks like this, which perhaps, depending on each of Your Honours' own personal preferences, might be the best single reference tool, because this really does take us down to the most relevant areas and it shows the most pertinent locations to the case. Let me just briefly, by way of orientation, mention some of the key locations. You have already heard reference to the villages of Sovici and Doljani. They are at the top of the map, and this map is oriented basically north, but at the top of the sheet would be basically north. We have Doljani and Sovici. You have the city of Mostar. You have, just to the north of the city of Mostar, Rastani, which you will hear about in the case. You have already heard about Siroki Brijeg, which is at this location. This was the location of Tuta's main headquarters. You will also hear testimony about the Heliodrom, which was a former Yugoslav Army base at a place called Rodoc, which is at this location. You will also hear about detention prisoners being detained at a place called Ljubuski, and you may hear, probably somewhat less so than the ones I've gone through in the last few minutes, but you may hear and will hear testimony that touches on Medugorje, Dretelj, Capljina. I think that's basically it. Again, a smaller version of these maps will be made available to the Chamber. There is also this document, which is smaller again, Exhibit 3.2, which is basically part of one of the larger maps. It does have some additional features, such as topographical lines, if that might be helpful. It sometimes tends to get perhaps a bit cluttered in comparison to this. But in any event, they are all available. What I would like to do now, Your Honours, is tell you how I anticipate proceeding with the balance of my Opening Statement. I will seek to provide Your Honours with an overview of the most relevant aspects of the Bosnian Croat / Bosnian Muslim conflict as they bear upon this case and to set this case in context. Certainly, and the Chamber will understand, literally hours, if not days, could be spent on the history, geography, political developments, military doctrine and other topics. Necessarily, I can only provide you today a very broad overview. When the overview is provided, I will then turn to the particular charges in the amended indictment and provide some additional outline of the Prosecution evidence. In proceeding this way, I do want to alert the Chamber, please, that there may be and in fact will be some repetition and overlap between, if you will, the first go-round and then the more specific review. But if I can respectfully say so, Your Honours, I think that perhaps some repetition is not such a major sin if it assists all of us and assists the Chamber in becoming oriented to the case. I will then, at the end of my opening, say a few words about how the Prosecution anticipates presenting its case. Now, returning to what this case is about, as with all cases at the ICTY, the story of this case begins with the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia. On the 25th of June, 1991, the former Republics of Croatia and Slovenia declared independence. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held a referendum and declared its independence in early March 1992. The crimes charged in this case occurred in the context of a wider conflict between the Bosnian Croat forces, which you will hear described as the Croatian Defence Council, or in short, "HVO," which in fact was more than just the army. One could say that the HVO was the army, the government, the administration and the executive branch of the self-declared Bosnian Croat state. You will hear repeatedly in the next days the term "HVO," and that is the Croatian Defence Council. You will also hear that this conflict, this wider conflict, was indeed actively supported and directed in some instances by the Army of the Republic of Croatia, which will be referenced often in short as the HV, "HV" simply being, in a nutshell, the Croatian alphabet language for the army of the Republic of Croatia, and that they were fighting-- these forces were allied against the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the duly-elected and established government based in Sarajevo. Those forces will often be referred to as the AbiH, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This conflict began as early as May 1992 in parts of Central Bosnia and continued until the signing of the Washington Agreement in February and March of 1994. The evidence at trial will show that the crimes committed by the accused and their subordinates in this case occurred as part of a wider campaign of persecution and ethnic cleansing directed by the HVO - the Croatian Defence Council - against Bosnian Muslims throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. The acts and omissions charged against these accused were part of a widespread, large-scale and systematic attack and campaign of persecution directed against the Bosnian Muslim population. During or before the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, a Croatian nationalist political party called the Croatian Democratic Union, or HDZ for short, was formed by former President Tudjman of Croatia and others in Croatia. It was this same nationalist HDZ party which ruled the Republic of Croatia from approximately 1991 until soon after President Tudjman's death in late 1999. A branch of this same party was formed among the Bosnian Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, called the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or again in short, the HDZ-BiH, or we will probably simply say "the HDZ," meaning either or both the Croatian parent and the Bosnian Croat child, if you will. Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the name indicates, is a country composed of at least two historical regions, the central and eastern part of the country called Bosnia, and the western or southwestern part of the country known as Herzegovina. This case primarily relates to Herzegovina. It is generally understood to include Southern Bosnia-Herzegovina, including essentially the municipalities previously identified. In fact, Herzegovina is larger than just those. Many of the other unmarked municipalities - that would be to the west and southwest of Sarajevo - would also be considered, of course, part of Herzegovina. But again, this will show you and does show you the most relevant municipalities which were part of Herzegovina and part of this case. On November 18th, 1991, the HDZ and the Bosnian Croats declared the existence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or, again, the HZ H-B for short. I'm reminded, as I hear myself, that I'm giving the Court many abbreviations and terms. I'm trying to pick only the most important, and I can only tell the Chamber you will hear these terms repeatedly. We will refer to it primarily as either just, in short, Herceg-Bosna or the HZ H-B. Essentially what happened, Your Honours, is that certain of the Bosnian Croats - we don't suggest for a minute all Bosnian Croats - but a nationalist, more extreme set of the Bosnian Croats declared this -- essentially self-declared existence of an independent or republic or entity of the Bosnian Croats on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina called the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It was claimed to be, in its own declaration, a separate political, cultural, economic and territorial whole in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Its purposes included, the Prosecution would submit, the establishment of closer ties to and perhaps ultimately annexation or union with the Republic of Croatia. These aspirations, which were supported by the Republic of Croatia, were evidenced by the HZ H-B's use of Croatian currency, the Croatian language, Croatian curriculum in the schools, and the granting by the Republic of Croatia of Croatian citizenship to Bosnian Croats. The Court should know that in fact the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina declared the HZ H-B illegal in September of 1992. Not deterred by this, the HZ H-B now declared itself not just the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna but now declared itself the Croatian Republic of Herzegovina on the 28th of August, 1993. In other words, the word "Community" was changed to the word "Republic." As I said earlier, for the purposes of this case, we will often refer to that whole entity as simply Herceg-Bosna. Neither of these entities were ever recognised by the International Community as legitimate states. And as I mentioned already, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina declared it illegal. Now, the city of Mostar is the historical capital and the largest city of Herzegovina. Article 3 of the HZ H-B proclamation of 18 November 1991 designated Mostar as the capital of this community. That is, the Bosnian Croats, or at least this part of them, declared their capital not to be Sarajevo but to be Mostar. This designation of Mostar was reaffirmed by the decree issued by the President of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban, on 8 April 1992, which also set up this entity you've heard about already, the Croatian Defence Council, or HVO. This was described and acted as the supreme executive, administrative and defence body of Herceg-Bosna, again with its headquarters in Mostar. These facts are important, Your Honours, because much of the evidence in this case will relate to the city of Mostar and the terrible things that happened there. As just indicated, the evidence will make it clear that the HVO considered Mostar their capital. And in the view of many of them, there was no room in Mostar for Muslims. I have already described to you that despite the name "Croatian Defence Council," it in fact served a wide number of executive and governmental purposes. I would also make the Chamber aware, if it is not already, that while the name was the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO in fact for a substantial period of time had a substantial number of Bosnian Muslim members, not just Croats but Muslims in its membership, because indeed the evidence will show, and I think history establishes this and I suspect it would not be disputed in this case - I would hope not - that for many months after the war started in Yugoslavia, of course, the Croats and Muslims fought together against their then-common enemy, the Serbs. And during that time, as I mentioned, there were in fact many Muslims in the HVO. Many of them remained there until well into 1993. And in fact, the Trial Chamber will hear testimony of several Bosnian Muslim members of the HVO who were still in the HVO in the spring and early summer of 1993, until they were disarmed, arrested and imprisoned by their very former Croat friends and allies. Despite being allies against the Serbs, the evidence will show that in fact tensions grew between the Croats and Muslims throughout 1992. In October of 1992, a conflict occurred between the HVO and Bosnian Muslims at Prozor. During the latter part of 1992 and the first several months of 1993, there were increasing tensions between the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims. And I should stop here to say another term in reference to the Bosnian Muslims is often used, and that is "Bosniaks." Respectfully, Your Honour, I and perhaps most of the Prosecution team will use the terms probably interchangeably, with no disrespect intended to either reference. In my experience in Bosnia, people use both interchangeably. Sometimes we may say "Bosniak," which means a Bosnian Muslim, and sometimes we will say "Bosnian Muslim." In any event, the fighting grew, the tensions were growing between the Croats and the Bosniaks, and again in some instances armed conflict began breaking out, again such as in Prozor in 1992 and in Gornji Vakuf, in Busovaca, in January 1993. Things, if you will, were coming undone. By the first few months of 1993, the Bosnian Croats, Muslims and Serbs had been engaged for some time, under the sponsorship of the International Community, in a series of peace negotiations concerning what was known or became known as the Vance-Owen Plan. By approximately late March of 1993, the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims had either signed or expressed their intent to sign the Vance-Owen Plan. In fact, the Bosnian Serbs, the third party, never did accept or sign the Plan. The evidence will show - and the reason I mention this in Opening Statement - the evidence will show that the Bosnian Croats, who for whatever reason were favourably positioned in the Vance-Owen Plan, became impatient with further steps to implement the plan, and in early April the President of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban, issued an ultimatum to the Muslims. That ultimatum was this: "Do not proceed with implementing the Vance-Owen plan." And the Muslim forces in certain municipalities or cantons did not subordinate and allow themselves to be taken over by the HVO. "If you do not do that, Muslims, by the 15th of April, 1993, then we will do it by force." I mentioned to you the 15th of April, 1993, and you will note already, of course, that the attack on Rastani led by the accused Tuta occurred on the 17th of April, 1993, two days after the ultimatum expired. In fact, in the first half of April, the Bosnian-Croat Muslim tensions escalated to higher, more dangerous levels. In the Herzegovinian municipalities of Stolac, Capljina, and Mostar, the HVO arrested prominent Bosnian Muslims and imposed various forms of persecution against the Bosnian-Muslim population such as dismissals from government and work positions, discrimination in the delivery of humanitarian aid, attacks against Bosnian-Muslim houses and property, an imposition of the Croat language and education. As I mentioned, the date of Mate Boban's ultimatum, 15th of April, 1993, passed without the HVO being satisfied. Accordingly, on the 16th of April, 1993, the HVO launched a large-scale offensive against the army at Bosnia-Herzegovina and against the Bosnian-Muslim population in general, starting in Central Bosnia in the municipalities of Vitez and Busovaca. Indeed, the 16th of April, 1993, is one of the most widely known dates of the entire war. Because it was on the 16th of April, 1993, that HVO units controlled by Tihomir Blaskic and Dario Kordic, both adjudged guilty in this Tribunal, massacred approximately 100 Bosnian-Muslim civilians in the village of Ahmici, near Vitez in Central Bosnia. Two days later, on the 18th of April, 1993, HVO units carried out a series of coordinated attacks against the Muslims in the Kiseljak municipality just north of Sarajevo. The purpose of the HVO attacks on Bosnian Muslims in Central Bosnia was to facilitate the establishment of an ethnically-homogenous or Croat-dominated entity on a territory of a sovereign country, that is Bosnia-Herzegovina, of what the HDZ and the HVO Croats called Herceg-Bosna. The crimes committed in Central Bosnia in furtherance of that objective have been the subject of several cases in this Tribunal, leading to the judgments in the Blaskic case, Kordic, Aleksovski, Kupreskic, and the Furundzija cases. The reason, or one reason, why this is important is because the evidence in this case will show, Your Honours, that the crimes committed by these accused, Naletilic and Martinovic, were part and parcel of the same plan, pursuing the same objectives as was being carried out by others in Central Bosnia. You will hear evidence that both Tuta's state of mind and his conduct were consistent with and in furtherance of this plan and objectives. You will hear testimony that Tuta considered that Muslims were nothing more than "Croats of Muslim faith." On the 17th of April, only one day after Ahmici, the day after Ahmici, as part of this same HVO plan, the accused Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, attacked the villages of Sovici and Doljani. After the attack was completed, the HVO forces expelled and evicted the Bosnian-Muslim population and destroyed their houses and a local mosque. On the 9th of May, the HVO, including the Convicts' Battalion, the unit that Tuta commanded, launched a large military offensive against the Bosnian Muslims and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Mostar. The Bosnian-Muslim population was thereafter a target of a systematic campaign of violence, persecution, and ethnic cleansing in the area of Mostar occupied by the HVO, which was called West Mostar. And this conduct lasted into the early part of 1994. Now, what you will find, and what you will begin hearing virtually immediately, is that the city of Mostar essentially became split between the Muslim Mostar and East Mostar and the Croat Mostar, which was West Mostar, a condition that essentially continued throughout the war. And in fact, in some respects, unfortunately, is largely the case still today. Across the confrontation line, that is in East Mostar, that part of Mostar was besieged by the HVO in a Sarajevo-like siege and suffered the most horrible and extreme conditions, including constant shelling, sniping, and the obstruction or blocking of humanitarian aid into that part of the city. The evidence will show that the accused, Naletilic, as one of the top HVO leaders in Herzegovina and commander of the Convicts' Battalion, his subordinate, the accused Vinko Martinovic, Stela, was the commander of one part of the Convicts' Battalion first called the Mrmak, later changed to Vinko Skrobo, ATG, anti-terrorist group unit of the Convicts' Battalion. The evidence will show that both Tuta and Stela were among the leading perpetrators of this campaign against Bosnian Muslims. The goal of the HVO's overall campaign in Herzegovina was to gain control of the various municipalities which they claimed to be part of Herceg-Bosna including, again, Mostar, Jablanica, Stolac, and others, and to either force the Bosnian-Muslim population to leave these territories entirely, or at least that they were reduced to complete subjugation of the Bosnian Croats. The means used to accomplish these ends included mass expulsions, detentions and imprisonments, killings, beatings, torture, evictions, destruction of cultural and religious heritage, looting, and deprivation of basic civil and human rights. These steps or means were executed following a systematic and wide pattern of ethnic, religious, and political discrimination. As a result of this campaign, in fact, tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslims were forced out of their homes. They were forced out of Mostar or forced into East Mostar under increasingly horrible conditions. In fact, as a result of the HVO onslaught, the traditional ethnic diversity in many parts of this region was virtually eliminated. And the Bosnian-Croat government was imposed. That is the wider context of the crimes committed, or alleged to be convicted [sic] which have been charged against these accused. The accused Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic are charged with crimes committed during 1993, early 1994, as part of this large-scale HVO ethnic cleansing campaign. Some of the crimes alleged in the indictment were perpetrated personally by each of the accused. Many other crimes were perpetrated by their subordinates, by their officers and soldiers under their control and subject to being either prevented in their conduct or punished for their conduct. But indeed, the evidence will show that far from punishing soldiers for war crimes, both the accused Tuta and the accused Martinovic led by example, and not a good example, but led by committing atrocities by their own hand. The Convicts' Battalion, the evidence will show, was, in the Croatian language, called Kaznjenicka Bojna, which can be translated again to be either Convicts' Battalion or Punishment Battalion. The Chamber will also hear it at times referred to as simply "Tuta's men" or the "Tutici". The battalion was comprised of several hundred solders divided into smaller units. The most notorious of these units was the so-called anti-terrorist groups, or, again, another abbreviation for you, ATGs. A very general short chart, again, to orient the Chamber on the structure. It has been placed on the ELMO. The Prosecution's evidence will show that the Kaznjenicka Bojna was the overall military unit; again, sometimes known by "Tuta's men" or other references. The commander was the accused Tuta. The main headquarters of this unit was in Siroki Brijeg at what had been a tobacco factory. The subunits -- you might call them companies, platoons, whatever unit-- the subunits of the battalion were, again, the ATGs, also some other subunits, but we are focusing here primarily on these so-called anti-terrorist groups. The evidence will show that one of these anti-terrorist groups was the group commanded by the second accused, Vinko Martinovic, Stela. He was the commander who was first known and referenced as the Mrmak ATG, which later changed its name to the Vinko Skrobo ATG. Its headquarters was in West Mostar, not very far from the confrontation line that divided Mostar. You will also hear testimony and receive evidence in the case that the Convicts' Battalion also had other bases, as some already mentioned, in Siroki Brijeg, Mostar, a place called the Heliodrom, and in Ljubuski. Next thing on the ELMO has been marked for identification as Exhibit 26.9. This shows, in fact, what was the former tobacco factory in Siroki Brijeg, and this was the main base for the Convicts' Battalion and the accused Tuta's principal headquarters. The evidence will show that the Convicts' Battalion was what some might call a special unit. They were very well equipped; they were very aggressive. It was used as an assault force, what some people might use the term, shock troops. They were sent into the most difficult situations, and they were notorious for being involved in the dirtiest jobs, including attacks on and expulsion of Bosnian Muslim civilians and destroying their homes and villages and plundering their property. The evidence will show that the accused Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was born on the 1st of December, 1946 in Siroki Brijeg, or what was then called Listica, now known as Siroki Brijeg. He is by birth a Bosnian-Croat who later acquired and has citizenship of the Republic of Croatia. The evidence will show that Naletilic, Tuta, in fact, was one of the top Bosnian-Croat leaders in all of Herzegovina with ready access to and dealings with other members, both political and military, of the top Bosnian-Croat hierarchy. You will hear how Tuta met with the key leaders of the Bosnian-Croat, of Herceg-Bosna. In fact, you will hear how he had direct links with senior officials in the Republic of Croatia. You will hear evidence that Tuta regularly travelled to Croatia, in fact, to meet with the Croatian Minister of Defence Gojko Susak, and that Susak likewise travelled a number of times to Naletilic's headquarters in Siroki Brijeg. Second accused, of course, is Vinko Martinovic, Stela. He was born on 21st of September, 1963 in Mostar. He is, again, a Bosnian-Croat by birth who also has acquired Croatian -- that is, citizenship in the Republic of Croatia. He was at all times material to this case a commander, again, of the ATG Mrmak, which later changed its name to the ATG Vinko Skrobo, and, of course, he was Tuta's subordinate. In any of the HVO units, and for that matter, the units on all sides, these units had their own patches and insignia. This was a patch worn by the soldiers of the members of the Vinko Skrobo ATG, which you will then see on the bottom part of the badge in the blue ribbon, again, the -- on the right side Kaznjenicka Bojna, Military Convicts' Battalion. The evidence will show that this unit, commanded by Martinovic, was in a section of West Mostar or near the confrontation line along a line on the Bulevar, and that his headquarters was in a building on Kalemova Street. You will hear much more about this as the trial proceeds. The accused are charged under both 7.1 and 7.3 of the Tribunal Statute, in all the counts on which they are charged. Of course, as Your Honours will know, individual criminal responsibility under Article 7.1 involves planning, instigating, ordering, committing or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation of execution of the acts or omissions charged in the amended indictment. Under Article 7.3, on the other hand, a superior -- in this case, a superior military officer -- is responsible for the acts of his or her subordinates if the superior knew or had reason to know that his or her subordinate was about to commit a crime or had done so, and the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish them afterwards. In terms of Article 7.3, responsibility, the evidence will show that Mladen Naletilic was the commander of the Convicts' Battalion and, in all respects acted as its military superior. He was involved in planning and carrying out its military operations. He oversaw and managed its finances and logistics. He coordinated its dealings and operations with other HVO units and also units of the Republic of Croatia. He exercised his authority over members of the Convicts' Battalion by meeting with his direct subordinates, his senior officers, and subcommanders on virtually a daily basis. He frequently interacted with the rank and file soldiers. He visited various Convicts' Battalion bases of operation; and indeed, he acted as a field commander himself on various occasions. The evidence will show that the HVO officers knew of the laws and rules of war, such as the Geneva Conventions, and that Tuta had the ability to both prevent and punish his subordinates' conduct. Again as indicated earlier, Vinko Martinovic was the commander of the Convicts' Battalion called the ATG Vinko Skrobo. He, in turn, exercised superior military authority over his unit and soldiers, both separately and in coordination with other HVO forces. As with Tuta, Stela had the ability to prevent and punish his soldiers' conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I hate to interrupt you, but would you please slow down a little bit. It is a very difficult time to the interpreter and the typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My apologies. The Trial Chamber will hear evidence of crimes committed by several of the more notorious subordinates of Naletilic and Martinovic who were members of the Convicts' Battalion. For instance, the Chamber will hear evidence concerning a man named Ivan Andabak, who was the deputy commander of the Convicts' Battalion. The Trial Chamber will also hear about several of Tuta's more notorious subordinates, such as Ernest Takac, Dinko Knezovic, and Romeo Blazevic. With that additional background, as I indicated before, allow me please to circle back to, again, Sovici and Doljani. On the 17th of April, 1993, again, only after one day after Ahmici, the accused Tuta led the Convicts' Battalion and other HVO forces on an attack on the villages of Sovici and Doljani in north central Herzegovina. Sovici and Doljani are two small villages located close to one another in a remote mountain area. According to the 1991 census, Sovici had 745 inhabitants, of which approximately 70 percent were Bosnian Muslims. The same census indicated that Doljani had approximately 1.000 inhabitants, and approximately 70 percent of that village being Croat. On the morning of the 17th of April, 1993, the attack on Sovici began. A small number of Bosnian Muslims attempted to defend the village. There will be no dispute about that. But they surrendered after only a few hours. HVO soldiers, including members of the Convicts' Battalion, entered Sovici on the afternoon of 17 April, captured AbiH soldiers were held at the Sovici school, along with other Muslim men of military age and, ultimately, also elderly, women, and children. A few photographs, again, to orient you. This is a photograph of the valley that contains Sovici and Doljani. As you can see, it is a relatively remote mountain area. I apologize for the glare. I don't know if it's as bad on everyone's monitors as they are on this. This is an aerial view again of Sovici, Doljani. Even though these photographs were taken some time later, I think by the indication here, 1999, unless the glare prevents it, you can see a huge number of the houses are still destroyed; the roofs blown off or the houses burned down. The aerial view of the location around the Sovici school. Parts of the village around the Sovici school. Cemetery here. The Sovici school is here, at which at one point approximately 450 Muslim civilians, including women and children, were kept in the school, the Sovici school. Little bit different angle. Close up again of the school, showing, again, the Sovici school, the middle photograph. There has been evidence already in the depositions that were taken some weeks ago, in addition to these people being held at the Sovici school, that five Muslim men were taken behind the school and executed. As I indicated, in the days following the takeover, the successful attack, the civilian inhabitants, the women, the children, the elderly, were forced out of their homes and kept in Sovici with the men. During this time, the houses of Bosnian Muslim inhabitants were burned, and a Sovici mosque was destroyed. This is after the attack was over. Systematic burning and destruction of property and religious institutions. After the capture of Sovici and Doljani, an HVO command post was established at a house in a small fish farm situated between the two villages. Naletilic was present at the command post. Indeed, it was his command post, or at least one of them. Photograph of what is marked as Exhibit 8.9 shows the house and the fish farm. You will see the pools. These facilities were used to raise fish. There was at the time in question an additional building on this side, which I am pointing to now, which has either been destroyed or fallen down or been removed since the 17th of April, 1993. The Chamber will hear evidence that many of the captured or arrested Muslim men were taken to the fish farm where they were mistreated and beaten and tortured, including, again, by the accused Tuta himself. After several days, many of the men were removed from the village and taken by buses to a prison at Ljubuski, which I have indicated to you before and shown you on the map. I won't stop now to show the map again, but taken to Ljubuski. The Bosnian Muslim women and children of Sovici and Doljani were removed from their villages and taken to approximately six abandoned houses in the nearby village of Junuzovici. They were forced to live in these houses for several days until they were taken by the HVO by truck to AbiH territory near Gornji Vakuf in central Bosnia. The evidence will show that they were essentially removed from the trucks and buses and left standing on the side of the road to fend for themselves, to find their way to friendly territory. In the following weeks, prisoners at the Ljubuski prison endured regular beatings and mistreatment and were forced to perform labour for Naletilic, including at his private estate, his own private estate, and the construction of a swimming pool near Siroki Brijeg. Eventually, many of these prisoners were transferred to the vast HVO Heliodrom detention complex located at Rodoc, approximately 6 kilometres south of Mostar. Here they joined thousands of Bosnian-Muslim prisoners from throughout the region where they continued to suffer mistreatment at the Heliodrom and were taken from the Heliodrom to perform forced labour on the confrontation line in Mostar. The Chamber will hear extensive evidence about that.
